resources.title: Scientific Notation
resources.subject: math
resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Scientific Notation - OK, How Does it Work? - Example: 700 - Example: 4,900,000,000 - Example: It is about 385,000,000 m from the Earth to the Moon - Try It Yourself - Other Ways of Writing It - Example: 3 × 10^4 is the same as 3 × 104 - Example: 6E+5 is the same as 6 × 105 - Example: 3.12E4 is the same as 3.12 × 104 - How to Do it - Example: 0.0055 is written 5.5 × 10-3 - Example: 3.2 is written 3.2 × 100 - Check! - Why Use It? - Example: it is easier to write (and read) 1.3 × 10-9 than 0.0000000013 - Example: a tiny space inside a computer chip has been measured to be 0.00000256m wide, 0.00000014m long and 0.000275m high. - Example: Suns, Moons and Planets - Play With It! - Engineering Notation - Examples: - Example: 0.00012 is written 120 × 10-6 Scientific Notation h1 Scientific Notation Scientific Notation (also called Standard Form in Britain) is a special way of writing numbers: It makes it easy to use very large or very small values. h2 OK, How Does it Work? h3 Example: 700 Why is 700 written as 7 × 102 in Scientific Notation ? 700 = 7 × 100 and 100 = 102 (see powers of 10) so 700 = 7 × 102 Both 700 and 7 × 102 have the same value, just shown in different ways. h3 Example: 4,900,000,000 1,000,000,000 = 109 , so 4,900,000,000 = 4.9 × 109 in Scientific Notation h3 Example: It is about 385,000,000 m from the Earth to the Moon 100,000,000 = 108 , 385,000,000 = 3.85 × 108 in Scientific Notation The number is written in two parts: - Just the digits, with the decimal point placed after the first digit, followed by - × 10 to a power that puts the decimal point where it should be (i.e. it shows how many places to move the decimal point). In this example, 5326.6 is written as 5.3266 × 103, because 5326.6 = 5.3266 × 1000 = 5.3266 × 103 h2 Try It Yourself Enter a number and see it in Scientific Notation: images/sci-notation.js Now try to use Scientific Notation yourself: images/sci-notation-num.js h2 Other Ways of Writing It 3.1 × 10^8 We can use the ^ symbol (above the 6 on a keyboard), as it is easy to type. h3 Example: 3 × 10^4 is the same as 3 × 104 3 × 10^4 = 3 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 30,000 Calculators often use "E" or "e" like this: h3 Example: 6E+5 is the same as 6 × 105 6E+5 = 6 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 600,000 h3 Example: 3.12E4 is the same as 3.12 × 104 3.12E4 = 3.12 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 31,200 h2 How to Do it To figure out the power of 10, think "how many places do I move the decimal point?" When the number is 10 or greater, the decimal point has to move left, and the power of 10 is positive. When the number is smaller than 1, the decimal point has to move right, so the power of 10 is negative. h3 Example: 0.0055 is written 5.5 × 10-3 Because 0.0055 = 5.5 × 0.001 = 5.5 × 10-3 h3 Example: 3.2 is written 3.2 × 100 We didn't have to move the decimal point at all, so the power is 100 But it is now in Scientific Notation After putting the number in Scientific Notation, just check that: - The "digits" part is between 1 and 10 (it can be 1, but never 10 or more) - The "power" part shows exactly how many places to move the decimal point h2 Why Use It? Because it makes it easier when dealing with very big or very small numbers, which are common in Scientific and Engineering work. h3 Example: it is easier to write (and read) 1.3 × 10-9 than 0.0000000013 It can also make calculations easier, as in this example: h3 Example: a tiny space inside a computer chip has been measured to be 0.00000256m wide, 0.00000014m long and 0.000275m high. What is its volume? Let us first convert the three lengths into scientific notation: - width: 0.000 002 56m = 2.56×10-6 - length: 0.000 000 14m = 1.4×10-7 - height: 0.000 275m = 2.75×10-4 Then multiply the digits together (ignoring the ×10s): 2.56 × 1.4 × 2.75 = 9.856 Last, multiply the ×10s: 10-6 × 10-7 × 10-4 = 10-17 (easier than it looks, just add −6, −4 and −7 together) The result is 9.856×10-17 m3 It is used a lot in Science: h3 Example: Suns, Moons and Planets Our Sun has a Mass of

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Second Derivative - Example: f(x) = x3 - Example: (continued) - Distance, Speed and Acceleration - Example: A bike race! - Play With It Second Derivative h1 Second Derivative A derivative basically gives you the slope of a function at any point. The derivative of 2x is 2 Read more about derivatives if you don't already know what they are! The "Second Derivative" is the derivative of the derivative of a function. So: - Find the derivative of a function - Then find the derivative of that A derivative is often shown with a little tick mark: f'(x) The second derivative is shown with two tick marks like this: f''(x) h3 Example: f(x) = x3 - The derivative of x3 is 3x2, so: - The derivative of 3x2 is 6x, so: A derivative can also be shown as and the second derivative shown as h3 Example: (continued) The previous example can also be written like this: h2 Distance, Speed and Acceleration A common real world example of this is distance, speed and acceleration: h3 Example: A bike race! You are cruising along in a bike race, going a steady 10 m every second. Distance: is how far you have moved along your path. It is common to use s for distance (from the Latin "spatium"). Speed: is how much your distance s changes over time t ... ... and is the first derivative of distance with respect to time: And we know you are doing 10 m per second, so: Acceleration: Now you start cycling faster! You increase your speed to 14 m every second over the next 2 seconds. When you are accelerating your speed is changing over time. is changing over time! We could write it like this: But it is usually written Your speed increases by 4 m/s over 2 seconds, so: In other words your speed changes by 2 meters per second per second. And yes, "per second" is used twice! It can be thought of as (m/s)/s but is usually written m/s2 (Note: in the real world your speed and acceleration change moment to moment, but here we assume you are super steady!) Here it is in one table: First Derivative is Speed: Second Derivative is Acceleration: But wait, there is more! The third derivative of position with respect to time (how acceleration changes over time) is called "Jerk" or "Jolt" ! We can actually feel Jerk when we start to accelerate, apply brakes or go around corners as our body adjusts to the new forces. Engineers try to reduce Jerk when designing elevators, train tracks, and so on. - The fourth derivative of position with respect to time is called "Snap" or "Jounce" - The fifth is "Crackle" - The sixth is "Pop" Yes, really! They go: distance, speed, acceleration, jerk, snap, crackle and pop h2 Play With It Here you can see the derivative f'(x) and the second derivative f''(x) of some common functions. images/function-graph-2deriv.js Notice how the slope of each function is the y-value of the derivative plotted below it. For example, move to where the sin(x) function slope flattens out (slope=0), then see that the derivative graph is at zero. A similar thing happens between f'(x) and f''(x). resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Second Order Differential Equations - Differential Equation - Order - Example: - Example: - Example: - Second Order Differential Equations - e to the rescue - Example 1: Solve - Check - So, does this method work generally? - Two Real Roots - Example 2: Solve - Example 3: Solve - Example 4: Solve - One Real Root - Example 5: Solve -   - How does this work in the general case? - Example 6: Solve - Complex roots - Example 7: Solve - Check - How do we generalize this? - Example 8: Solve - Example 9: Solve - Summary Second Order Differential Equations h1 Second Order Differential Equations Here we learn how to solve equations of this type: Differential Equation Differential Equation is a n equation with a function and one or more of its derivatives: Example: an equation with the function y and its derivative The Order is the highest derivative (is it a first derivative? a second derivative? etc): It has only the first derivative , so is "First Order" + xy = sin(x) This has a second derivative , so is "Second Order" or "Order 2" This has a third derivative which outranks the , so is "Third Order" or "Order 3" Before tackling second order differential equations, make sure you are familiar with the various methods for solving first order differential equations. h2 Second Order Differential Equations We can solve a second order differential equation of the type: + Q(x)y = f(x) where P(x), Q(x) and f(x) are functions of x, by using: Undetermined Coefficients which only works when f(x) is a polynomial, exponential, sine, cosine or a linear combination of those, or Variation of Parameters which is a little messier but works on a wider range of functions. But here we begin by learning the case where f(x) = 0 (this makes it "homogeneous"): and also where the functions P(X) and Q(x) are constants p and q: Let's learn to solve them! h3 e to the rescue We are going to use a special property of the derivative of the exponential function: At any point the slope (derivative) of ex equals the value of ex : And when we introduce a value "r" like this: - the first derivative is f'(x) = rerx - the second derivative is f''(x) = r2erx In other words, the first and second derivatives of f(x) are both multiples of f(x) This is going to help us a lot! h3 Example 1: Solve Let y = erx so we get: Substitute these into the equation above: r2erx + rerx − 6erx = 0 erx(r2 + r − 6) = 0 r2 + r − 6 = 0 We have reduced the differential equation to an ordinary quadratic equation! This quadratic equation is given the special name of characteristic equation. We can factor this one to: (r − 2)(r + 3) = 0 So r = 2 or −3 And so we have two solutions: But that’s not the final answer because we can combine different multiples of these two answers to get a more general solution: y = Ae2x + Be−3x Let us check that answer. First take derivatives: y = Ae2x + Be−3x = 2Ae2x − 3Be−3x = 4Ae2x + 9Be−3x Now substitute into the original equation: (4Ae2x + 9Be−3x) + (2Ae2x − 3Be−3x) − 6(Ae2x + Be−3x) = 0 4Ae2x + 9Be−3x + 2Ae2x − 3Be−3x − 6Ae2x − 6Be−3x = 0 4Ae2x + 2Ae2x − 6Ae2x+ 9Be−3x− 3Be−3x − 6Be−3x = 0 h2 So, does this method work generally? resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Seismic Waves - Learning from Seismic Waves - Body Waves - Surface Waves - Seismograph Seismic Waves h1 Seismic Waves Seismic waves travel through the earth. They are caused by: - Earthquakes - Large explosions - Some mining works - Atomic blasts - etc This truck vibrates the ground! The waves can be detected some distance away and tell us about the structure of the ground. h2 Learning from Seismic Waves Earthquakes are extremely powerful and can travel great distances. They are destructive, but have also helped us learn that the earth is made of a crust, mantle and outer and inner core as shown here: The Earth has different zones. Scientists have studied how the earth reacts to wave movement. Patterns of wave motion provide information about the properties and structure of earth’s materials. Waves created by people (through explosions or impact) are used to draw pictures of the internal structure and layering underground, and are useful in locating potential oil wells. The different zones affect how seismic waves travel. Waves show different motion patterns as they move from one zone to the next, thus allowing zones to be located, described, and their depths determined. h2 Body Waves When seismic waves are first created, they travel outwards in all direction from their source. Body waves travel through the interior of the earth, and have two main types: - P-Waves (Primary waves) are Longitudinal Waves. - S-Waves (Secondary waves) are Transverse Waves. images/waves.js P-Waves are fastest at about 6 km/s (kilometers per second) and arrive first. They can travel through solids, liquids, and gases and pass right through the Earth in a special pattern. S-Waves are slower at about 3.6 km/s and arrive second. They can only pass through solids and so cannot pass through the earth’s liquid core. Scientists noticed that seismic stations on opposite sides of the earth would never receive S-waves (giving evidence that the outer core is in fact a liquid). Timing when each wave arrives at a seismic station can help locate an earthquake. h2 Surface Waves There are two main types of surface waves: - Love Waves, which move the ground from side-to-side. They are the fastest surface wave. - Rayleigh Waves, which roll along the ground like an ocean wave. h2 Seismograph Seismographs record the arrival of earthquake waves. They operate using a shock absorbing or dampening system that allows a stabilized marker or pencil to chart the motion of the waves on paper (set on a rotating drum). The seismograph records the time of the arrival of the different types of waves. It also shows differences in their wave heights (called amplitude). The patterns in wave data is critical in determining the nature and location of the earthquake. When an earthquake occurs, the drum moves with the motion of the ground while rotating the paper. The marker is independent of this movement and records the pattern of motion as the paper/drum rotates underneath it. Pictured below is a sample seismograph (from the 1906 earthquake that hit San Francisco, USA). Notice the arrival of the P and S waves. Here is another seismograph showing surface waves, and with marks showing when the P-Wave and S-Wave arrived: Image courtesy Wikipedia user Crickett Timing when each wave arrives at a seismic station can help locate an earthquake. Once seismologists have the arrival times of earthquake waves from at least three stations, they can work backwards to determine the point of the epicenter. First, they find the P and S wave arrival times from three stations. The difference between the P and S arrival time for each station is matched with a distance on a travel-time graph (as below). The time interval can be found on the vertical axis of the graph, then held vertically and slid outward until it touches the S and P wave lines. Separation of Variables h1 Separation of Variables Separation of Variables is a special method to solve some Differential Equations A Differential Equation is an equation with a function and one or more of its derivatives: Example: an equation with the function y and its derivative h2 When Can I Use it? Separation of Variables can be used when: All the y terms (including dy) can be moved to one side of the equation, and All the x terms (including dx) to the other side. Three Steps: Move all the y terms (including dy) to one side of the equation and all the x terms (including dx) to the other side Integrate one side with respect to y and the other side with respect to x. Don't forget "+ C" (the constant of integration) h3 Example: Solve this (k is a constant): Separate the variables by moving all the y terms to one side of the equation and all the x terms to the other side: Multiply both sides by dx: Divide both sides by y: Integrate both sides of the equation separately: Put the integral sign in front: Integrate left side: Integrate right side: ln(y) + C = kx + D C is the constant of integration. And we use D for the other, as it is a different constant. We can roll the two constants into one (a=D−C): ln(y) = kx + a e(ln(y)) = y , so let's take exponents on both sides: And ekx + a = ekx ea so we get: is just a constant so we replace it with c: We have solved it: This is a general type of first order differential equation which turns up in all sorts of unexpected places in real world examples. We used y and x, but the same method works for other variable names, like this: h3 Example: Rabbits! The more rabbits you have the more baby rabbits you will get. Then those rabbits grow up and have babies too! The population will grow faster and faster. The important parts of this are: - the population N at any time t - the growth rate r - the population's rate of change The rate of change at any time equals the growth rate times the population: But hey! This is the same as the equation we just solved! It just has different letters: - N instead of y - t instead of x - r instead of k So we can jump to a solution: And here is an example, the graph of N = 0.3e2t Exponential Growth There are other equations that follow this pattern such as continuous compound interest. h2 More Examples OK, on to some different examples of separating the variables: h3 Example: Solve this: Separate the variables by moving all the y terms to one side of the equation and all the x terms to the other side: Multiply both sides by dx: dy = (1/y) dx Multiply both sides by y: Integrate both sides of the equation separately: Put the integral sign in front: Integrate each side: (y2)/2 = x + C We integrated both sides in the one line. We also used a shortcut of just one constant of integration C. This is perfectly OK as we could have +D on one, +E on the other and just say that C = E−D. Multiply both sides by 2: y2 = 2(x + C) Square root of both sides: y = ±√(2(x + C)) Note: This is not the same as y = √(2x) + C, because the C was added before we took the square root. This happens a lot with differential equations. We cannot just add the C at the end of the process. It is added when doing the integration. We have solved it: y = ±√(2(x + C)) A harder example: h3 Example: Solve this: Separate the variables: Multiply both sides by dx, divide both sides by y: Integrate both sides of the equation separately: The left side is a simple logarithm, the right side can be integrated using substitution: Let u = 1 + x2, so du = 2x dx: ln(y) = ln(u) + C Then we make C = ln(k): ln(y) = ln(u) + ln(k) So we can get this: Now put u = 1 + x2 back again: y = k(1 + x2) It is already as simple as can be. Let's find the differences: 1st Difference: 2nd Difference: The first differences change, but the second differences (the differences of the differences) are all 2. resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Sequences - What's a Sequence? - Infinite or Finite - Examples: - In Order - Like a Set - Notation - A Rule - As a Formula - So, What Can A Rule For {3, 5, 7, 9, ...} Be? - Many Rules - Example: the sequence {3, 5, 7, 9, ...} - Notation For Rules - Special Sequences - Arithmetic Sequences - Example: - Geometric Sequences - Example: - Triangular Numbers - Square Numbers - Cube Numbers - Fibonacci Sequence - Series and Partial Sums - Example: Odd numbers h1 Sequences You can read a gentle introduction to Sequences in Common Number Patterns. h2 What's a Sequence? A Sequence is a list of things (usually numbers) that are in order. h2 Infinite or Finite When the sequence goes on forever it is called an infinite sequence, otherwise it is a finite sequence h3 Examples: {1, 2, 3, 4, ...} is a very simple sequence (and it is an infinite sequence) {20, 25, 30, 35, ...} is also an infinite sequence {1, 3, 5, 7} is the sequence of the first 4 odd numbers (and is a finite sequence) {4, 3, 2, 1} is 4 to 1 backwards {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...} is an infinite sequence where every term doubles {a, b, c, d, e} is the sequence of the first 5 letters alphabetically {f, r, e, d} is the sequence of letters in the name "fred" {0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, ...} is the sequence of alternating 0s and 1s (yes they are in order, it is an alternating order in this case) When we say the terms are "in order", we are free to define what order that's! They could go forwards, backwards ... or they could alternate ... or any type of order we want! h2 Like a Set A Sequence is like a Set, except: - the terms are in order (with Sets the order doesn't matter) - the same value can appear many times (only once in Sets) Example: {0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, ...} is the sequence of alternating 0s and 1s. The set is just {0,1} Sequences also use the same notation as sets: {3, 5, 7, ...} list each element, separated by a comma, and then put curly brackets around the whole thing. The curly brackets are sometimes called "set brackets" or "braces". A Sequence usually has a Rule, which is a way to find the value of each term. Example: the sequence {3, 5, 7, 9, ...} starts at 3 and jumps 2 every time: h2 As a Formula Saying "starts at 3 and jumps 2 every time" is fine, but it doesn't help us calculate the: - 10th term, - 100th term, or - nth term, where n could be any term number we want So, we want a formula with " " in it (where is any term number). h3 So, What Can A Rule For {3, 5, 7, 9, ...} Be? First, we can see the sequence goes up 2 every time, so we can guess that a Rule is something like "2 times n" (where "n" is the term number). Let's test it out: Test Rule: 2n 2n = 2×1 = 2 2n = 2×2 = 4 2n = 2×3 = 6 That nearly worked ... but it is too low by 1 every time, so let's try changing it to: Test Rule: 2n+1 2n+1 = 2×1 + 1 = 3 2n+1 = 2×2 + 1 = 5 2n+1 = 2×3 + 1 = 7 So instead of saying "starts at 3 and jumps 2 every time" we write this: Now we can calculate, for example, the 100th term: 2 × 100 + 1 = 201 h2 Many Rules But mathematics is so powerful we can often find more than one Rule that fits the same sequence. h3 Example: the sequence {3, 5, 7, 9, ...} We have just shown a Rule for {3, 5, 7, 9, ...} is: 2n + 1 This gives the sequence: {3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, ...} But can we find another rule that starts the same way? How about "odd numbers without a 1 in them": And we get: {3, 5, 7, 9, 23, 25, ...} The first few terms match, but then the sequence changes! And we could find more rules that match {3, 5, 7, 9, ...}. Really we could. That's why it is better to say "a rule" rather than "the rule", unless we are sure which rule is intended. h2 Notation For Rules To make it easier to use rules, we often use this special style: - xn is the term - n is the term number Example: to mention the "5th term" we write: So a rule for {3, 5, 7, 9, ...} can be written as an equation like this: And to calculate the 10th term we can write: x10 = 2n+1 = 2×10+1 = 21 Can you calculate (the 50th term) doing thi

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Sequences - Finding a Rule - Sequence - Finding Missing Numbers - Example: 1, 4, 9, 16, ? - Example: 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ? - Many Rules - What is the next number in the sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, ? - Simplest Rule - Finding Differences - Second Differences - Other Types of Sequences Sequences - Finding A Rule h1 Sequences - Finding a Rule To find a missing number in a Sequence, first we must have a Rule A Sequence is a set of things (usually numbers) that are in order. Each number in the sequence is called a term (or sometimes "element" or "member"), read Sequences and Series for a more in-depth discussion. h2 Finding Missing Numbers To find a missing number, first find a Rule behind the Sequence. Sometimes we can just look at the numbers and see a pattern: h3 Example: 1, 4, 9, 16, ? Answer: they are Squares (12=1, 22=4, 32=9, 42=16, ...) Rule: xn = n2 Sequence: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, ... Did you see how we wrote that rule using "x" and "n" ? xn means "term number n", so term 3 is written x3 And we can calculate term 3 using: We can use a Rule to find any term. For example, the 25th term can be found by "plugging in" 25 wherever n is. x25 = 252 = 625 How about another example: h3 Example: 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ? After 3 and 5 all the rest are the sum of the two numbers before, That is 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13 and so on, which is part of the Fibonacci Sequence: 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89, ... Which has this Rule: Rule: xn = xn-1 + xn-2 Note: This kind of rule needs the first two terms to get started (in this case 3 and 5). Now what does xn-1 mean? It means "the previous term" as term number n-1 is 1 less than term number n. And xn-2 means the term before that one. Let's try that Rule for the 6th term: x6 = x6-1 + x6-2 x6 = x5 + x4 So term 6 equals term 5 plus term 4. We already know term 5 is 21 and term 4 is 13, so: x6 = 21 + 13 = 34 h2 Many Rules One of the troubles with finding "the next number" in a sequence is that mathematics is so powerful we can find more than one Rule that works. h3 What is the next number in the sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, ? Here are three solutions (there can be more!): Solution 1: Add 1, then add 2, 3, 4, ... So, 1+1=2, 2+2=4, 4+3=7, 7+4=11, and so on... Rule: xn = n(n-1)/2 + 1 Sequence: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, ... (That rule looks a bit complicated, but it works) Solution 2: After 1 and 2, add the two previous numbers, plus 1: Rule: xn = xn-1 + xn-2 + 1 Sequence: 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, ... Solution 3: After 1, 2 and 4, add the three previous numbers Rule: xn = xn-1 + xn-2 + xn-3 Sequence: 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, 24, 44, ... So, we have three perfectly reasonable solutions, and they create totally different sequences. Which is right? They are all right. And there are other solutions ... ... it may be a list of the winners' numbers ... so the next number could be ... anything! h2 Simplest Rule To choose a rule confidently, we usually need more terms or some real-world context (what the numbers mean). When in doubt choose the simplest rule that makes sense, but also mention that there are other solutions. h2 Finding Differences Sometimes it helps to find the differences between each pair of numbers ... this can often reveal an underlying pattern. Here is a simple case: The differences are always 2, so we can guess that "2n" is part of the answer. Let us try 2n: The last row shows that we are always wrong by 5, so just add 5 and we are done: Rule: xn = 2n + 5 OK, we could have worked out "2n+5" by just playing around with the numbers a bit, but we want a systematic way to do it, for when the sequences get more complicated. h2 Second Differences In the sequence {1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, ...} we need to find the differences ... ... and then find the differences of those (called second differences), like this: When the second differences are constant, the rule involves , and also half of the second difference. resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Set-Builder Notation - Type of Number - Number Types - Why Use It? - Another Example: - Example: x ≤ 2 or x > 3 - Defining a Domain - Example: The domain of 1/x - Example: The domain of g(x)=1/(x−1) - Example: The domain of √x - Example The domain of f(x) = x/(x2 − 1) Set-Builder Notation h1 Set-Builder Notation How to describe a set by saying what properties its members have. A Set is a collection of things (usually numbers). Example: {5, 7, 11} is a set. But we can also "build" a set by describing what is in it. Here is a simple example of set-builder notation: It says "the set of all x's, such that x is greater than 0". In other words any value greater than 0 - The "x" is just a place-holder, it could be anything, such as { q | q > 0 } - Some people use ":" instead of "|", so they write { x : x > 0 } h2 Type of Number It is also normal to show what type of number x is, like this: - The means "a member of" (or simply "in") - The is the special symbol for Real Numbers "the set of all x's that are a member of the Real Numbers, such that x is greater than or equal to 3" In other words "all Real Numbers from 3 upwards" There are other ways we could have shown that: On the Number Line it looks like: In Interval notation it looks like: [3, +∞) h2 Number Types (the special symbol for Real Numbers). Here are the common number types: Natural Numbers Rational Numbers Real Numbers Imaginary Numbers Complex Numbers "the set of all k's that are a member of the Integers, such that k is greater than 5" In other words all integers greater than 5. This could also be written {6, 7, 8, ... } , so: = {6, 7, 8, ... } h2 Why Use It? When we have a simple set like the integers from 2 to 6 we can write: {2, 3, 4, 5, 6} But how do we list the Real Numbers in the same interval? {2, 2.1, 2.01, 2.001, 2.0001, ... ??? So instead we say how to build the list: | x ≥ 2 and x ≤ 6 } Start with all Real Numbers, then limit them between 2 and 6 inclusive. We can also use set builder notation to do other things, like this: | x = x2 } = {0, 1} All Real Numbers such that x = x2 0 and 1 are the only cases where x = x2 h2 Another Example: h3 Example: x ≤ 2 or x > 3 Set-Builder Notation looks like this: | x ≤ 2 or x >3 } On the Number Line it looks like: Using Interval notation it looks like: (−∞, 2] U (3, +∞) We used a "U" to mean Union (the joining together of two sets). h2 Defining a Domain Set Builder Notation is very useful for defining domains. In its simplest form the domain is the set of all the values that go into a function. The function must work for all values we give it, so it is up to us to make sure we get the domain correct! h3 Example: The domain of 1/x 1/x is undefined at x=0 (because 1/0 is dividing by zero). So we must exclude x=0 from the Domain: The Domain of 1/x is all the Real Numbers, except 0 We can write this as Dom(1/x) = {x | x ≠ 0} h3 Example: The domain of g(x)=1/(x−1) 1/(x−1) is undefined at x=1, so we must exclude x=1 from the Domain: The Domain of 1/(x−1) is all the Real Numbers, except 1 Using set-builder notation it is written: Dom( g(x) ) = { | x ≠ 1} h3 Example: The domain of √x Is all the Real Numbers from 0 onwards, because we can't take the square root of a negative number (unless we use Imaginary Numbers, which we aren't). We can write this as Dom(√x) = {x | x ≥ 0} h3 Example The domain of f(x) = x/(x2 − 1) To avoid dividing by zero we need: x2 - 1 ≠ 0 Factor: x2 - 1 = (x−1)(x+1) (x−1)(x+1) = 0 when x = 1 or x = −1, which we want to avoid! Dom( f(x) ) = {x | x ≠ 1, x ≠ −1} 7211, 551, 552, 1187, 1188, 7212, 553, 1189, 1190, 554 Algebra Index Copyright © 2025 Rod Pierce

Here are the most common set symbols In the examples C = {1, 2, 3, 4} and D = {3, 4, 5} Set: a collection of elements {1, 2, 3, 4} Union: in A or B (or both) D = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} Intersection: in both A and B Subset: every element of A is in B. resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Set of All Points That ... - Example: A Circle is: - Locus - Example: An ellipse is the locus of points whose distance from two fixed points add up to a constant. Set of All Points h1 Set of All Points That ... In Mathematics we often say "the set of all points that ... ". What does it mean? A set is just a collection of things with some common property. When we collect ALL points that share a property we can end up with a line, a surface or other interesting thing. Points can make a line h3 Example: A Circle is: "the set of all points on a plane that are a fixed distance from a central point". So, just a few points start to look like a circle, but when we collect ALL the points we will actually have a circle. Try drawing one yourself (move any point): images/geom-locus.js (Note: the points are drawn as dots so you can see them, but they really should have no size at all) Imagine this happening in 3D space: all the points that are a fixed distance from a center make a sphere! The idea of "the set of all points that ..." is used so much it has a name: Locus. A Locus is a set of points that share a property. So, a circle is "the locus of points on a plane that are a fixed distance from the center". Note: "Locus" usually means that the points make a continuous curve or surface. h3 Example: An ellipse is the locus of points whose distance from two fixed points add up to a constant. So, no matter where we are on the ellipse, we can add up the distance to point "F" and to point "G" and it will always be the same result. (The points "F" and "G" are called the foci of the ellipse) The idea of "Locus" can be used to create some weird and wonderful shapes! 7922, 7923, 7924, 7925, 7926, 7927, 7928, 7929, 7930, 7931 Copyright © 2025 Rod Pierce

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Sets and Venn Diagrams - Sets - Ten Best Friends - Union - Intersection - Which Way Does That "U" Go? - Difference - Summary So Far - Three Sets - Universal Set - Complement - Summary Sets and Venn Diagrams h1 Sets and Venn Diagrams A set is a collection of things. For example, the items you wear is a set: these include hat, shirt, jacket, pants, and so on. You write sets inside curly brackets like this: {hat, shirt, jacket, pants, ...} You can also have sets of numbers: - Set of whole numbers: {0, 1, 2, 3, ...} - Set of prime numbers: {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, ...} h2 Ten Best Friends You could have a set made up of your ten best friends: - {alex, blair, casey, drew, erin, francis, glen, hunter, ira, jade} Each friend is an "element" (or "member") of the set. It is normal to use lowercase letters for them. Now let's say that alex, casey, drew and hunter play Soccer: Soccer = {alex, casey, drew, hunter} (It says the Set "Soccer" is made up of the elements alex, casey, drew and hunter.) And casey, drew and jade play Tennis: Tennis = {casey, drew, jade} We can put their names in two separate circles: You can now list your friends that play Soccer OR Tennis. This is called a "Union" of sets and has the special symbol ∪: Soccer ∪ Tennis = {alex, casey, drew, hunter, jade} Not everyone is in that set ... only your friends that play Soccer or Tennis (or both). In other words we combine the elements of the two sets. We can show that in a "Venn Diagram": Venn Diagram: Union of 2 Sets A Venn Diagram is clever because it shows lots of information: - Do you see that alex, casey, drew and hunter are in the "Soccer" set? - And that casey, drew and jade are in the "Tennis" set? - And here is the clever thing: casey and drew are in BOTH sets! All that in one small diagram. h2 Intersection "Intersection" is when you must be in BOTH sets. In our case that means they play both Soccer AND Tennis ... which is casey and drew. The special symbol for Intersection is an upside down "U" like this: ∩ And this is how we write it: Soccer ∩ Tennis = {casey, drew} In a Venn Diagram: Venn Diagram: Intersection of 2 Sets h3 Which Way Does That "U" Go? Think of them as "cups": holds more water than , right? is the one with more elements than Intersection ∩ h2 Difference You can also "subtract" one set from another. For example, taking Soccer and subtracting Tennis means people that play Soccer but NOT Tennis ... which is alex and hunter. And this is how we write it: Soccer − Tennis = {alex, hunter} In a Venn Diagram: Venn Diagram: Difference of 2 Sets h2 Summary So Far - ∪ is Union: is in either set or both sets - ∩ is Intersection: only in both sets - − is Difference: in one set but not the other h2 Three Sets You can also use Venn Diagrams for 3 sets. Let us say the third set is "Volleyball", which drew, glen and jade play: Volleyball = {drew, glen, jade} But let's be more "mathematical" and use a Capital Letter for each set: - S means the set of Soccer players - T means the set of Tennis players - V means the set of Volleyball players The Venn Diagram is now like this: Union of 3 Sets: S ∪ T ∪ V You can see (for example) that: - drew plays Soccer, Tennis and Volleyball - jade plays Tennis and Volleyball - alex and hunter play Soccer, but don't play Tennis or Volleyball - no-one plays only Tennis We can now have some fun with Unions and Intersections ... This is just the set S S = {alex, casey, drew, hunter} This is the Union of Sets T and V T ∪ V = {casey, drew, jade, glen} This is the Intersection of Sets S and V S ∩ V = {drew} And how about this ... - take the previous set S ∩ V - then subtract T: This is the Intersection of Sets S and V minus Set T (S ∩ V) − T = {} Hey, there is nothing there! That is OK, it is just the "Empty Set". It is still a set, so we use the curly brackets with nothing inside: {} The Empty Set has no elements: {} h2 Universal Set The Universal Set is the set that has everything. resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Shared Birthdays - Friends and Random Numbers - First, what is the chance that Alex and Billy have the same number? -   - Now, let's include Chris ... - Now what happens when we include Dusty? - Example: what are the chances that with 6 people any of them celebrate their Birthday in the same month? (Assume equal months) - There are 30 people in a room ... what is the chance that any two of them celebrate their birthday on the same day? Assume 365 days in a year. - Simulation - For Real Shared Birthdays h1 Shared Birthdays This is a great puzzle, and you get to learn a lot about probability along the way ... There are 30 people in a room ... what is the chance that any two of them celebrate their birthday on the same day? Assume 365 days in a year. Some people may think: "there are 30 people, and 365 days, so 30/365 sounds about right. That makes 30/365 = 0.08..., so about 8% maybe?" The probability is much higher. It is actually likely there are people who share a birthday in that room. Because you should compare everyone to everyone else. And with 30 people that is 435 comparisons. But you also have to be careful not to over-count the chances. I will show you how to do it ... starting with a smaller example: h2 Friends and Random Numbers 4 friends (Alex, Billy, Chris and Dusty) each choose a random number between 1 and 5. What is the chance that any of them chose the same number? We will add our friends one at a time ... h3 First, what is the chance that Alex and Billy have the same number? Billy compares his number to Alex's number. There is a 1 in 5 chance of a match. As a tree diagram: Note: "Yes" and "No" together make 1 (1/5 + 4/5 = 5/5 = 1) h3 Now, let's include Chris ... But there are now two cases to consider (called "Conditional Probability"): - If Alex and Billy did match, then Chris has only one number to compare to - But if Alex and Billy did not match then Chris has two numbers to compare to And we get this: For the top line (Alex and Billy did match) we already have a match (a chance of 1/5). But for the "Alex and Billy did not match" case there are 2 numbers that Chris could match with, so there is a 2/5 chance of Chris matching (against both Alex and Billy). And a 3/5 chance of not matching. And we can work out the combined chance by multiplying the chances it took to get there: Following the "No, Yes" path ... there is a 4/5 chance of No, followed by a 2/5 chance of Yes: (4/5) × (2/5) = 8/25 Following the "No, No" path ... there is a 4/5 chance of No, followed by a 3/5 chance of No: (4/5) × (3/5) = 12/25 Also notice that adding all chances together is 1 (a good check that we haven't made a mistake): (5/25) + (8/25) + (12/25) = 25/25 = 1 h3 Now what happens when we include Dusty? It is the same idea, just more of it: OK, that is all 4 friends, and the "Yes" chances together make 101/125: Answer: 101/125 But here is something interesting ... if we follow the "No" path we can skip all the other calculations and make our life easier: The chances of not matching are: (4/5) × (3/5) × (2/5) = 24/125 So the chances of matching are: 1 − (24/125) = 101/125 (And we didn't really need a tree diagram for that!) And that is a popular trick in probability: It is often easier to work out the "No" case (and subtract from 1 for the "Yes" case) h3 Example: what are the chances that with 6 people any of them celebrate their Birthday in the same month? (Assume equal months) The "no match" case for: - 2 people is 11/12 - 3 people is (11/12) - 4 people is (11/12) - 5 people is (11/12) - 6 people is (11/12) So the chance of not matching is: (7/12) = 0.224... Flip that around and we get the chance of matching: 1 − 0.224... = 0.776... So, there is a 77.6% chance of any of them celebrating their Birthday in the same month And now we can try calculating the "Shared Birthday" question we started with: There are 30 people in a room ... what is the chance that any two of them celebrate their birthday on the same day? resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Showing the Results of a Survey - Tables - Statistics - Graphs - People's Comments - Report Showing the Results of a Survey h1 Showing the Results of a Survey When we have Conducted a Survey and want to show our results clearly and engagingly we have lots of choices: Sometimes, we can simply report the information in a table. A table is a very simple way to show the results. A table should have a title, so those looking at it understand what it shows: Table: The Favorite Colors of My Class h2 Statistics We can also summarize the results using statistics such as Mean, Median, Mode, Standard Deviation and Quartiles Example: we have lots of information about how long it takes people to get to school but it may be simpler just to present a summary such as: Shortest Journey: 3 minutes Average Journey: 22 minutes Longest Journey: 58 minutes But nothing makes a report look better than a nice graph or chart. There are many different types of graphs. Here are some choices: Bar Graph – shows relative sizes of different results: Line Graph - shows information that is somehow connected (such as change over time): Pie Chart - shows sizes as part of a whole (good for showing percentages): shows data using dots We can create graphs like those using Data Graphs (Bar, Line, Pie and Dot). h2 People's Comments If people have given their opinions or comments in the survey, we can present the more interesting ones: Example: In response to the question "How can we best clean up the river?" we received these interesting replies: - "The government has a special fund for this" - "The local gardening group has seedlings we could plant" Put it all together into a report, with a nice introduction, and conclusions at the end, and we are done! resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Similar Triangles - Corresponding Sides - Calculating the Lengths of Corresponding Sides - Example: Find lengths a and b of Triangle S - Step 1: Find the ratio - Step 2: Use the ratio Similar Triangles h1 Similar Triangles Two triangles are Similar if the only difference is size (and possibly the need to turn or flip one around). These triangles are all similar: (Equal angles have been marked with the same number of arcs) Note: as well as different sizes, some of them are turned or flipped. For similar triangles: All corresponding angles are equal All corresponding sides have the same ratio Also notice that the corresponding sides face the corresponding angles. For example the sides that face the angles with two arcs are corresponding sides. h2 Corresponding Sides In similar triangles, corresponding sides are always in the same ratio. For example: Triangles R and S are similar. The equal angles are marked with the same numbers of arcs. What are the corresponding lengths? - The lengths 7 and a are corresponding (they face the angle marked with one arc) - The lengths 8 and 6.4 are corresponding (they face the angle marked with two arcs) - The lengths 6 and b are corresponding (they face the angle marked with three arcs) h2 Calculating the Lengths of Corresponding Sides We can sometimes calculate lengths we don't know yet. - Step 1: Find the ratio of corresponding sides - Step 2: Use that ratio to find the unknown lengths h3 Example: Find lengths a and b of Triangle S h3 Step 1: Find the ratio We know all the sides in Triangle R, and We know the side 6.4 in Triangle S The 6.4 faces the angle marked with two arcs as does the side of length 8 in triangle R. So we can match 6.4 with 8, and so the ratio of sides in triangle S to triangle R is: 6.4 to 8 Now we know that the lengths of sides in triangle S are all 6.4/8 times the lengths of sides in triangle R. h3 Step 2: Use the ratio a faces the angle with one arc as does the side of length 7 in triangle R. a = (6.4/8) × 7 = 5.6 b faces the angle with three arcs as does the side of length 6 in triangle R. b = (6.4/8) × 6 = 4.8 Did You Know? Similar triangles can help you estimate distances. 736, 737, 738, 1526, 1527, 1528, 3951, 3952, 3953, 3954 Finding Similar Triangles Similar Triangle Theorems Congruent Triangles Trigonometry Index Copyright © 2025 Rod Pierce

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Simplify - What's the Simplest Form? - How to Simplify - And Which Is Simpler Here? Simplify: to make simpler! One of the big jobs we do in Algebra is simplification. You will often be asked to put something "in simplest form" h2 What's the Simplest Form? In general, it is simpler when it is easier to use. 5x + x − 3 Combine like terms: 6x − 3 It is now a little easier to use. We can simplify the fraction: Divide top and bottom by 3: "Half" is definitely simpler than "three sixths", unless it is important to know that something was cut into sixths. Multiply the constants and variables: It is now a little easier to use. 2x2 − 6x + 2x − 3 Polynomial long division: 2x − 3 x2 − 2x − 3 (x−3)(x+1) That last example can be argued with! Some people say to remove parentheses to make it "simpler", but (x−3)(x+1) is usually a lot easier to use. The moral of the story: "Simplified" is sometimes obvious, but can also depend on what you want to do. h2 How to Simplify There are many ways to simplify! When we simplify we use similar skills to solving equations, and that page has some good advice. Some of these things might help: - Combine Like Terms - Factor - Expand (the opposite of factoring) - Clear out fractions by multiplying - Find some pattern you have seen before, like the difference of squares h2 And Which Is Simpler Here? Here's one more interesting case: √ seems simple enough √ has a rationalized denominator (normally considered simpler, and preferred by teachers!) Which is simpler? You decide! 8709, 8710, 8711, 8712, 8713, 8714, 8715, 8716, 8717, 8718, 8719, 8720 Algebra Index Copyright © 2026 Rod Pierce

Here's the rule: when a and b are not negative √ √ × √ Why no negatives? Square roots of negative numbers aren't real, so the rule would break. And here's how to use it: h3 Example: simplify √12 12 is 4 times 3: √12 = √(4 × 3) Use the rule: √(4 × 3) = √4 × √3 And the square root of 4 is 2: √4 × √3 = 2√3 So √12 is simpler as 2√3 h3 Example: simplify √45 √45 45 is 9 times 5: √(9 × 5) Use the rule: √9 × √5 The square root of 9 is 3: 3√5 So √45 is simpler as 3√5 More examples: h3 Example: simplify √8 √8 = √(4×2) = √4 × √2 = 2√2 (Because the square root of 4 is 2) h3 Example: simplify √18 √18 = √(9 × 2) = √9 × √2 = 3√2 It often helps to factor the numbers (into prime numbers is best): h3 Example: simplify √6 × √15 First we can combine the two numbers: √6 × √15 = √(6 × 15) Then we factor them: √(6 × 15) = √(2 × 3 × 3 × 5) Then we see two 3s, and decide to "pull them out": √(2 × 3 × 3 × 5) = √(3 × 3) × √(2 × 5) = 3√10 h2 Addition or Subtraction? h3 Do not use the rule for addition or subtraction √(a + b) is not equal to √a + √b √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 But if we split them up: √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7 Different answer! So don't split up addition or subtraction inside a square root. h2 Fractions But we can use a similar rule for fractions: √ √ √ h3 Example: simplify √30√10 First we can combine the two numbers: √30√10 √( Then simplify: √( = √3 h2 Some Harder Examples h3 Example: simplify √20 × √5√2 √20 × √5√2 Factor 20 into 2 × 2 × 5: √(2 × 2 × 5) × √5√2 Break into separate square roots: √2 × √2 × √5 × √5√2 Cancel a √2 from top and bottom: √2 × √5 × √5 √5 × √5 = 5: √2 × 5 5√2 h3 Example: simplify 2√12 + 9√3 First simplify 2√12: 2√12 = 2 × 2√3 = 4√3 Now both terms have √3, we can add them: 4√3 + 9√3 = (4+9)√3 = 13√3 A root we can't simplify further is called a Surd. (get your calculator out and check them!) h3 Example: what are the sine, cosine and tangent of 45° ? The classic 45° triangle has two sides of 1 and a hypotenuse of √ sin(45°) = 1 / 1.414 = 0.707... cos(45°) = 1 / 1.414 = 0.707... tan(45°) = 1 / 1 = 1 h2 Why? resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Sine Function - Graph Exercise - Sine Function - Draw Triangles - Step 1: Draw the Angled Lines - Step 2: Draw and Measure the Triangles - Measure Triangles - Graph The Results - Result Sine Function - Graph Exercise h1 Sine Function - Graph Exercise The Sine Function produces a very beautiful curve, but don't take our word for it, make your own! h2 Sine Function First, read the page on Sine, Cosine and Tangent. Now you will know that the sine of any angle is the length of the far side of the triangle (the "opposite") divided by the long side (the "hypotenuse"): Sine of θ = Opposite / Hypotenuse h2 Draw Triangles To make the graph, we need to calculate the sine for different angles, then put those points on a graph, and then "join the dots". h3 Step 1: Draw the Angled Lines Place a mark at the center of a piece of paper, then, using a protractor, mark every 15 degrees from 0° to 180° in a semi-circle. Then rotate the protractor and mark from 180° around to the start again. Then draw lines radiating from the center to each of your marks so that you end up with an illustration like this: Lines at 15° (click to enlarge) Or, you can click on the above illustration, then print out the result. h3 Step 2: Draw and Measure the Triangles We can now turn each of those lines into a triangle, example: h2 Measure Triangles When you have completed each triangle, it is simply a matter of measuring the lines. Remember that the sine is the length of the line opposite the angle divided by the hypotenuse (which should all be the same length if you have drawn it well) Write all your measurements in a table. This is what I got, but your measurements may be different: Opposite / Hypotenuse 0.00 0.26 0.50 etc ... You can print a table ready to fill in here. Important: When the "opposite" line goes downwards it is negative. Tip: if you have drawn it well, you can take advantage of the symmetry of 0−90, 90−180, 180−270 and 270−360. h2 Graph The Results Get some graph paper and prepare it by scaling off 0 to 360 in 15 increments along the x-axis, and scaling off −1 to +1 on the y-axis. You can use your own graph paper, or print out this graph paper Now plot each point from the table on the graph. Then join the dots as neatly as you can. The result should look something like the graph at the very top. But you have done much more than draw a nice curve. You have : - learned about one of the most important functions in mathematics - learned that you don't have to believe what people say - you can try it for yourself - had experience plotting graphs - learned how symmetry can save effort We hope you had a great time exploring! resources.subject: math
resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Skewed Data - Negative Skew? - The Normal Distribution has No Skew - Positive Skew - Example: Income Distribution - Calculating Skewness h1 Skewed Data Data can be "skewed", meaning it tends to have a long tail on one side or the other: Negative Skew Positive Skew h2 Negative Skew? Why is it called negative skew? Because the long "tail" is on the negative side of the peak. Some people say it is skewed left, meaning the long tail is on the left hand side In a negative skew, the measures of central tendency are pulled in different directions: - The Mode is at the highest peak - The Median is left of the peak - The Mean is pulled furthest left by the long tail So: Mean < Median < Mode h2 The Normal Distribution has No Skew A Normal Distribution isn't skewed. It is perfectly symmetrical. And the Mean is exactly at the peak. h2 Positive Skew And positive skew is when the long tail is on the positive side of the peak Some people say it is "skewed right". The mean is on the right of the peak value. h2 Example: Income Distribution Here's some data extracted from a recent Census. As you can see it is positively skewed ... in fact the tail continues way past $100,000 Quick Question: A bakery usually sells 10 to 15 cakes a day. But on a few holiday days they sell over 100 cakes. Is this data skewed left (negative) or right (positive)? It is skewed right (positive skew), because the rare high-sales days create a long tail on the positive (right) side of the graph. h2 Calculating Skewness "Skewness" (the amount of skew) can be calculated, for example you could use the SKEW() function in Excel or OpenOffice Calc. 8775, 8776, 8777, 8778, 8779, 8780, 8781, 8782, 8783, 8784 Normal Distribution Copyright © 2026 Rod Pierce

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Slope (Gradient) of a Straight Line - Examples: - Positive or Negative? - Straight Across - Straight Up and Down - Rise and Run Slope (Gradient) of a Straight Line h1 Slope (Gradient) of a Straight Line The slope (also called Gradient) of a line tells us how steep it is. To find the slope: Divide the vertical change (how far it goes up or down) by the horizontal change (how far it moves sideways). Change in YChange in X Have a play (drag the points): images/geom-line-equn.js?mode=slope h2 Examples: The slope of this line = So the slope is equal to 1 In other words for every 3 steps right, the line goes up 3 steps. Since both are the same, the slope is 1. The slope of this line = The line is steeper, and so the slope is larger. The slope of this line = = 0.6 The line is less steep, and so the slope is smaller. h2 Positive or Negative? Moving from left-to-right, the cyclist has to : - Nosedive on a Negative slope - Push up on a Positive slope When measuring the line: - Starting from the left and going across to the right is positive (but going across to the left is negative). - Up is positive, and down is negative That line goes down as you move along, so it has a negative slope. h2 Straight Across A line that goes straight across (Horizontal) has a slope of zero. h2 Straight Up and Down That last one is a bit tricky ... you can't divide by zero, so a "straight up and down" (vertical) line's slope is "undefined". h2 Rise and Run We also call the horizontal change "run", and the vertical change "rise" or "fall": They are just different words, none of the calculations change. 2068, 2069, 2070, 2071, 2072, 5316, 5317, 5318, 5319, 5320 Equation of a Straight Line Y Intercept of a Straight Line Test Yourself Straight Line Graph Calculator Copyright © 2025 Rod Pierce

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Slope of a Function at a Point - Instructions - Interesting Functions - Accuracy Slope of a Function at a Point h1 Slope of a Function at a Point Use this interactive to find the slope at a point. Instructions below. images/function-graph-slope.js h2 Instructions Type your function into the top box ... your function is plotted live. Now drag the points "A" and "B" to the function line. When they are close they will "snap" to the function. Bring points "A" and "B" near the point where you want to find the slope. When "A" and "B" are on top of each other the slope could be anything! So keep them a small distance apart. : by pressing "Fit". Now bring the points closer together. Keep zooming and moving the points closer together until you are happy with the answer. This is the idea behind differential calculus. We can't have a gap of zero (the slope could be anything), but as the gap heads towards zero, the slope heads towards the true slope at that point. h2 Interesting Functions Try finding the slope of - x = 1 - x = 2 - x = 3 Try finding the slope of - x = 1 - x = 1.5 - x = 2 Try finding the slope of - y = 1 (x=0) - y = 1.2 - y = 1.5 There are only a few hundred pixels in either direction, and so the calculations are not totally accurate. But they should give you a good feel for what is going on. And don't worry, you can often use differential calculus to find an accurate answer! resources.title: Solving AAS Triangles
resources.subject: math
resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Solving AAS Triangles - Example 1 - Example 2 Solving AAS Triangles h1 Solving AAS Triangles "AAS" means "Angle, Angle, Side" "AAS" is when we know two angles and one side (which is not between the angles). To solve an AAS triangle - use the three angles add to 180° to find the other angle - then The Law of Sines to find each of the other two sides h3 Example 1 In this triangle we know: - angle A = 35° - angle C = 62° - and side c = 7 We can first find angle B by using 'angles of a triangle add to 180°': B = 180° − 35° − 62° = 83° To find side a we can use The Law of Sines: a/sin(A) = c/sin(C) a/sin(35°) = 7/sin(62°) Multiply both sides by sin(35°): a = sin(35°) × 7/sin(62°) a = 4.55 to 2 decimal places To find side b we can also use The Law of Sines: b/sin(B) = c/sin(C) b/sin(83°) = 7/sin(62°) Multiply both sides by sin(83°): b = sin(83°) × 7/sin(62°) b = 7.87 to 2 decimal places Now we have completely solved the triangle! We used b/sin(B) = c/sin(C) rather than b/sin(B) = a/sin(A) for the last calculation ... why? There's a good reason for that. What if we made a mistake when finding a? Then our answer for b would also be wrong! As a rule, it is always better to use the sides and angles that are given rather than ones we've just worked out. h3 Example 2 This is also an AAS triangle. First find angle A by using "angles of a triangle add to 180°": A = 180° − 41° − 105° = 34° Now find side c by using The Law of Sines: c/sin(C) = b/sin(B) c/sin(41°) = 12.6/sin(105°) c = sin(41°) × 12.6/sin(105°) c = 8.56 to 2 decimal places Similarly we can find side a by using The Law of Sines and using the given side b = 12.6 (rather than side c that we just worked out): a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) a/sin(34°) = 12.6/sin(105°) a = sin(34°) × 12.6/sin(105°) a = 7.29 to 2 decimal places 261, 3956, 1540, 262, 1541, 1542, 1560, 2370, 2371, 3955 Triangle Solving Practice The Law of Sines The Law of Cosines Solving Triangles Trigonometry Index Algebra Index Copyright © 2025 Rod Pierce

To solve an ASA Triangle - find the third angle using the three angles add to 180° - then use The Law of Sines to find each of the other two sides h3 Example 1 In this triangle we know: - angle A = 76° - angle B = 34° - and c = 9 It's easy to find angle C by using 'angles of a triangle add to 180°': C = 180° − 76° − 34° = 70° We can now find side a by using the Law of Sines: a = sin(76°) × a = 9.29 to 2 decimal places Similarly we can find side b by using the Law of Sines: b = sin(34°) × b = 5.36 to 2 decimal places Now we have completely solved the triangle: we have found all angles and sides. h3 Example 2 This is also an ASA triangle. First find angle X by using 'angles of a triangle add to 180°': X = 180° − 87° − 42° = 51° Now find side y by using the Law of Sines: 18.9sin(51°) y = sin(87°) × 18.9sin(51°) y = 24.29 to 2 decimal places. resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Solving Equations - What's an Equation? - What's a Solution? - Example: x − 2 = 4 - More Than One Solution - Example: (x−3)(x−2) = 0 - Solutions Everywhere! - Example: sin(−θ) = −sin(θ) is one of the Trigonometric Identities - How to Solve an Equation - A Useful Goal - Example: Solve 3x−6 = 9 - Variables on Both Sides - Example: Solve 5x = 2x + 9 - Using Parentheses - Example: Solve 3(x + 2) = 15 - Like a Puzzle - Example: Solve √(x/2) = 3 - Special Equations - Check Your Solutions - How To Check - Example: solve for x: - Tips Solving Equations h1 Solving Equations h2 What's an Equation? An equation says two things are equal. It will have an equals sign "=" like this: That equations says: what's on the left (x − 2) equals what's on the right (4) So an equation is like a statement "this equals that" h2 What's a Solution? A Solution is a value we can put in place of a variable (such as ) that makes the equation true. which is true So x = 6 is a solution. How about other values for ? - For x=5 we get "5−2=4" which is not true, so x=5 isn't a solution - For x=9 we get "9−2=4" which is not true, so x=9 isn't a solution - and so on In this case x = 6 is the only solution. You might like to practice solving some animated equations. h2 More Than One Solution There can be more than one solution. h3 Example: (x−3)(x−2) = 0 (3−3)(3−2) = 0 × 1 = 0 which is true (2−3)(2−2) = (−1) × 0 = 0 which is also true So the solutions are: x = 3, or x = 2 When we gather all solutions together it is called a Solution Set The above solution set is: h2 Solutions Everywhere! Some equations are true for all allowed values and are then called Identities h3 Example: sin(−θ) = −sin(θ) is one of the Trigonometric Identities Let's try θ = 30°: sin(−30°) = −0.5 and −sin(30°) = −0.5 So it is true for θ = 30° Let's try θ = 90°: sin(−90°) = −1 and −sin(90°) = −1 So it is also true for θ = 90° Is it true for all values of θ? Try some values for yourself! h2 How to Solve an Equation There's no "one perfect way" to solve all equations. First follow the Golden Rule: to keep the balance, what we do to one side of the "=" we must also do to the other side. h3 A Useful Goal We often get success when our goal is to end up with: x = something In other words, we want to move everything except "x" (or whatever name the variable has) over right hand side. h3 Example: Solve 3x−6 = 9 Add 6 to both sides: Divide by 3: Now we have x = something, and a short calculation reveals x = 5 h3 Variables on Both Sides h3 Sometimes we have variables on both sides of the equals sign. We can move them just like we move numbers. h3 Example: Solve 5x = 2x + 9 h3 We want all the x's on one side. Subtract 2x from both sides: Divide by 3: h3 Using Parentheses h3 If an equation has parentheses, we can use the Distributive Law to expand it first. h3 Example: Solve 3(x + 2) = 15 Expand 3(x + 2): Subtract 6 from both sides: Divide by 3: h2 Like a Puzzle In fact, solving an equation is just like solving a puzzle. And like puzzles, there are things we can (and can't) do. Here are some things we can do: - Add or Subtract the same value from both sides - Clear out any fractions by Multiplying every term by the bottom parts - Divide every term by the same nonzero value - Combine Like Terms - Factoring - Expanding (the opposite of factoring) may also help - Recognizing a pattern, such as the difference of squares - Sometimes we can apply a function to both sides (e.g. square both sides) h3 Example: Solve √(x/2) = 3 Square both sides: Calculate 32 = 9: Multiply both sides by 2: And the more "tricks" and techniques you learn the better you will get. h2 Special Equations There are special ways of solving some types of equations. Learn how to ... - solve Quadratic Equations - solve Radical Equations - solve Equations with Sine, Cosine and Tangent h2 Check Your Solutions You should always check that your "solution" really is a solution. h3 How To Check Take the solution(s) and put them in the original

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Solving Inequalities - Solving - Example: x + 2 > 12 - How to Solve - Safe Things To Do - Example: 3x < 7+3 - Example: 2y+7 < 12 - Adding or Subtracting a Value - Example: x + 3 < 7 - What did we do? - What If I Solve It, But "x" Is On The Right? - Example: 12 < x + 5 - Multiplying or Dividing by a Value - Positive Values - Example: 3y < 15 - Negative Values - Why? - Example: −2y < −8 - Multiplying or Dividing by Variables - Example: bx < 3b - A Bigger Example - Example: x−32 < −5 - Two Inequalities At Once! - Example: - Summary Solving Inequalities h1 Solving Inequalities Sometimes we need to solve Inequalities like these: greater than greater than or equal to less than or equal to Our aim is to have (or whatever the variable is) on its own on the left of the inequality sign: Something like: We call that "solved". h3 Example: x + 2 > 12 Subtract 2 from both sides: x + 2 − 2 > 12 − 2 h2 How to Solve Solving inequalities is very like solving equations, we do most of the same things ... ... but we must also pay attention to the direction of the inequality. Direction: Which way the arrow "points" Some things can change the direction! h2 Safe Things To Do These things don't affect the direction of the inequality: - Add (or subtract) a number from both sides - Multiply (or divide) both sides by a positive number - Simplify a side h3 Example: 3x < 7+3 We can simplify 7+3 without affecting the inequality: these things do change the direction of the inequality ("<" becomes ">" for example): - Multiplying (or dividing) both sides by a negative number - Swapping left and right hand sides h3 Example: 2y+7 < 12 When we swap the left and right hand sides, we must also change the direction of the inequality: Here are the details: h2 Adding or Subtracting a Value We can often solve inequalities by adding (or subtracting) a number from both sides (just as in Introduction to Algebra), like this: h3 Example: x + 3 < 7 If we subtract 3 from both sides, we get: x + 3 − 3 < 7 − 3 And that's our solution: x < 4 In other words, x can be any value less than 4. h3 What did we do? We went from this: And that works well for adding and subtracting, because if we add (or subtract) the same amount from both sides, it doesn't affect the inequality Example: Alex has more coins than Billy. If both Alex and Billy get three more coins each, Alex will still have more coins than Billy. h2 What If I Solve It, But "x" Is On The Right? No matter, just swap sides, but reverse the sign so it still "points at" the correct value! h3 Example: 12 < x + 5 If we subtract 5 from both sides, we get: 12 − 5 < x + 5 − 5 That's a solution! But it is normal to put "x" on the left hand side ... ... so let's flip sides (and the inequality sign!): Do you see how the inequality sign still "points at" the smaller value (7) ? And that's our solution: x > 7 Note: "x" can be on the right, but people usually like to see it on the left hand side. h2 Multiplying or Dividing by a Value Another thing we do is multiply or divide both sides by a value (just as in Algebra - Multiplying). But we need to be a bit more careful (as you will see). Positive Values Everything is fine if we want to multiply or divide by a positive number: h3 Example: 3y < 15 If we divide both sides by 3 we get: And that's our solution: y < 5 Negative Values When we multiply or divide by a negative number we must reverse the inequality. resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Solving Inequality Word Questions - Sam and Alex play in the same soccer team. Last Saturday Alex scored 3 more goals than Sam, but together they scored less than 9 goals. What are the possible number of goals Alex scored? - Turning English into Algebra - Sam and Alex play in the same soccer team. Last Saturday Alex scored 3 more goals than Sam, but together they scored less than 9 goals. What are the possible number of goals Alex scored? - Lots More Examples! - Example: Of 8 pups, there are more girls than boys. How many girl pups could there be? - Example: Joe enters a race where he has to cycle and run. He cycles a distance of 25 km, and then runs for 20 km. His average running speed is half of his average cycling speed. Joe completes the race in less than 2½ hours, what can we say about his average speeds? - Example: The velocity v m/s of a ball thrown directly up in the air is given by v = 20 − 10t, where t is the time in seconds. At what times will the velocity be between 10 m/s and 15 m/s? - Example: A rectangular room fits at least 7 tables that each have 1 square meter of surface area. The perimeter of the room is 16 m. What could the width and length of the room be? Solving Inequality Word Questions h1 Solving Inequality Word Questions You might like to read Introduction to Inequalities and Solving Inequalities first. In Algebra we have "inequality" questions like: h3 Sam and Alex play in the same soccer team. Last Saturday Alex scored 3 more goals than Sam, but together they scored less than 9 goals. What are the possible number of goals Alex scored? How do we solve them? The trick is to break the solution into two parts: Turn the English into Algebra. Then use Algebra to solve. h2 Turning English into Algebra To turn the English into Algebra it helps to: - Read the whole thing first - Do a sketch if needed - Assign letters for the values - Find or work out formulas We should also write down what's actually being asked for, so we know where we are going and when we have arrived! The best way to learn this is by example, so let's try our first example: h3 Sam and Alex play in the same soccer team. Last Saturday Alex scored 3 more goals than Sam, but together they scored less than 9 goals. What are the possible number of goals Alex scored? Assign Letters: - the number of goals Alex scored: A - the number of goals Sam scored: S We know that Alex scored 3 more goals than Sam did, so: A = S + 3 And we know that together they scored less than 9 goals: S + A < 9 We are being asked for how many goals Alex might have scored: A A = S + 3, so: Subtract 3 from both sides: 2S < 9 − 3 Divide both sides by 2: Sam scored less than 3 goals, which means that Sam could have scored 0, 1 or 2 goals. Alex scored 3 more goals than Sam did, so Alex could have scored 3, 4, or 5 goals. - When S = 0, then A = 3 and S + A = 3, and 3 < 9 is correct - When S = 1, then A = 4 and S + A = 5, and 5 < 9 is correct - When S = 2, then A = 5 and S + A = 7, and 7 < 9 is correct - (But when S = 3, then A = 6 and S + A = 9, and 9 < 9 is incorrect) h2 Lots More Examples! h3 Example: Of 8 pups, there are more girls than boys. How many girl pups could there be? Assign Letters: - the number of girls: g - the number of boys: b We know that there are 8 pups, so: g + b = 8, which can be rearranged to b = 8 − g We also know there are more girls than boys, so: We are being asked for the number of girl pups: g b = 8 − g, so: 8 − g Add g to both sides: Divide both sides by 2: So there could be 5, 6, 7 or 8 girl pups. Look out for "hidden" rules in word questions. Some answers must be whole numbers, and "more than" can mean there's at least one of the other group. Could there be 8 girl pups? Then there would be no boys at all, and the question isn't clear on that point (sometimes questions are like that). - When g = 8, then b = 0 and g > b is correct (but is b = 0 allowed?) - When g = 7, then b = 1 and g > b is correct -

resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Solving Polynomials - Solving - Example: −2 and 2 are the roots of the function x2 − 4 - Degree - How To Solve - 1. Basic Algebra - Example: 2x + 1 - 2. By experience, or simply guesswork - Example: x3 + 2x2 − x - Example: x3−8 - 3. Graphically - Factors - Example: f(x) = (x3 + 2x2)(x − 3) - Common Mistakes to Avoid - Example: 3(2x − 4) - How to Check - Example: 2x3 − x2 − 7x + 2 - Example (continued): 2x3 − x2 − 7x + 2 - How Far Left or Right - Have We Got All The Roots? - Example: 2x3 + 3x − 6 - But Some Roots May Be Complex - Positive or Negative Roots? - Multiplicity of a Root - Example: f(x) = (x − 5)3(x + 7)(x − 1)2 - Example: f(x) = (x − 2)2(x − 4)3 - Summary Solving Polynomials h1 Solving Polynomials A polynomial looks like this: Example of a polynomial "Solving" means finding the "roots" ... ... a "root" (or "zero") is where the function is equal to zero: Between two neighboring real roots (x-intercepts), the function is either entirely above, or entirely below, the x-axis. So at a real root the polynomial's value is zero, indicating where its graph intersects the x-axis. h3 Example: −2 and 2 are the roots of the function x2 − 4 Let's check: - when x = −2, then x2 − 4 = (−2)2 − 4 = 4 − 4 = 0 - when x = 2, then x2 − 4 = 22 − 4 = 4 − 4 = 0 How do we solve polynomials? That depends on the Degree! The first step in solving a polynomial is to find its degree. The Degree of a Polynomial with one variable is ... ... the largest exponent of that variable. When we know the degree we can also give the polynomial a name: Graph Looks Like ... ... ... ... h2 How To Solve So now we know the degree, how to solve? - Read how to solve Linear Polynomials (Degree 1) using simple algebra - Read how to solve Quadratic Polynomials (Degree 2) with a little work, - Cubic (degree 3) and quartic (degree 4) polynomials can be tricky to solve, but there are special methods and formulas - Polynomials of degree 5 or higher have no simple formula that always works. We can sometimes factor them, or use numerical methods to approximate roots So what do we do with ones we can't solve? Try to solve them a piece at a time! If we find one root, we can then reduce the polynomial by one degree (example later) and this may be enough to solve the whole polynomial. Here are some main ways to find roots. h3 1. Basic Algebra We may be able to solve using basic algebra: h3 Example: 2x + 1 2x + 1 is a linear polynomial: The graph of y = 2x + 1 is a straight line It is linear so there's one root. Use Algebra to solve: A "root" is when y is zero: Subtract 1 from both sides: Divide both sides by 2: And that's the solution: (You can also see this on the graph) We can also solve Quadratic Polynomials using basic algebra (read that page for an explanation). h3 2. By experience, or simply guesswork It is always a good idea to see if we can do simple factoring: h3 Example: x3 + 2x2 − x This is cubic ... but wait ... we can factor out "x": x3 + 2x2 − x = x(x2 + 2x − 1) Now we have one root (x=0) and what's left is quadratic, which we can solve exactly. The above is an equation (=) but sometimes we need to solve inequalities like these: greater than greater than or equal to less than or equal to 2y2 + 1 ≤ 7y Solving inequalities is very like solving equations ... we do most of the same things. When solving equations we try to find points, such as the ones marked "=0" But when solving inequalities we try to find interval(s), such as the ones marked ">0" or "<0" So this is what we do: - find the "=0" points - in between the "=0" points, are intervals that are either - greater than zero (>0), or - less than zero (<0) - then pick a test value to discover which it is (>0 or <0) Here's an example: h3 Example: x2 − x − 6 < 0 x2 − x − 6 has these simple factors (what luck!): (x+2)(x−3) < 0 First, let's find where it is equal to zero: It is equal to zero when x = −2 or x = +3 because when x = −2, then (x+2) is zero or when x = +3, then (x−3) is zero So between −2 and +3, the function will either be - always greater than zero, or - always less than zero We don't know which ... yet! Let's pick a value in-between (say x=0) and test it: substitute x=0: So between x=−2 and x=+3, the function is less than zero. And that's the region we want, so... x2 − x − 6 < 0 in the interval Note: x2 − x − 6 0 in the interval (−∞,−2) and (3, +∞) And here's the graph of x2 − x − 6: - The equation equals zero at −2 and 3 - The inequality "<0" is true between −2 and 3 Also try the Inequality Grapher. h2 What If It Doesn't Go Through Zero? Here's the graph of x2 − x + 1 There are no "=0" points! But that makes things easier. Because the line doesn't cross through y=0, it must be either: - always > 0, or - always < 0 So all we have to do is test one value (say x=0) to see if it is above or below. h2 A "Real World" Example h3 A stuntman will jump off a 20 m building. A high-speed camera is ready to film him between 15 m and 10 m above the ground. When should the camera film him? We can use this formula for distance and time: d = 20 − 5t2 - d = distance above ground (m), and - t = time from jump (seconds) (Note: if you are curious about the formula, it is simplified from d = d0 + v0t + ½a0t2 , where d0=20, v0=0, and a0=−9.81 the acceleration due to gravity.) First, let's subtract 20 from both sides: −10 < −5t2 <−5 Now multiply both sides by −(1/5). To be neat, the smaller number should be on the left, and the larger on the right. resources.excerpt: ## 目录要点 - Solving Radical Equations - Radical Equations - Solving Radical Equations - Example: solve √(2x+9) − 5 = 0 - More Than One Square Root - Example: solve √(2x−5) − √(x−1) = 1 Solving Radical Equations h1 Solving Radical Equations How to solve equations with square roots, cube roots, etc. h2 Radical Equations A Radical Equation is an equation with a square root or cube root, etc. h2 Solving Radical Equations We can get rid of a square root by squaring (or cube roots by cubing, etc). Warning: this can sometimes create "solutions" which don't actually work when we put them into the original equation. So we need to Check! Follow these steps: - isolate the square root on one side of the equation - square both sides of the equation Then continue with our solution! h3 Example: solve √(2x+9) − 5 = 0 isolate the square root: square both sides: Now it should be easier to solve! Move 9 to right: 2x = 25 − 9 = 16 Divide by 2: x = 16/2 = 8 Check: √(2·8+9) − 5 = √(25) − 5 = 5 − 5 = 0 That one worked perfectly. h2 More Than One Square Root What if there are two or more square roots? Easy! Just repeat the process for each one. It will take longer (lots more steps) ... but nothing too hard. h3 Example: solve √(2x−5) − √(x−1) = 1 isolate one of the square roots: √(2x−5) = 1 + √(x−1) square both sides: 2x−5 = (1 + √(x−1))2 We have removed one square root. expand right hand side: 2x−5 = 1 + 2√(x−1) + (x−1) 2x−5 = 2√(x−1) + x subtract x from both sides: x−5 = 2√(x−1) Now do the "square root" thing again: isolate the square root: √(x−1) = (x−5)/2 square both sides: x−1 = ((x−5)/2)2 We have now successfully removed both square roots. Let us continue on with the solution. Expand right hand side: x−1 = (x2 − 10x + 25)/4 It is a Quadratic Equation! So let us put it in standard form. Multiply by 4 to remove division: 4x−4 = x2 − 10x + 25 Bring all to left: 4x − 4 − x2 + 10x − 25 = 0 Combine like terms: −x2 + 14x − 29 = 0 Swap all signs: x2 − 14x + 29 = 0 Using the Quadratic Formula (a=1, b=−14, c=29) gives the solutions: 2.53 11.47 (to 2 decimal places) Let us check the solutions: 2.53 : √(2×2.53−5) − √(2.53−1) ≈ −1 Oops! Should be plus 1. 11.47 : √(2×11.47−5) − √(11.47−1) ≈ 1 Yes that one works. There is really only one solution: Answer: 11.47 (to 2 decimal places) See? This method can sometimes produce solutions that don't really work! The root that seemed to work, but wasn't right when we checked it, is called an "Extraneous Root" So checking is important. 8079, 8080, 8081, 8082, 575, 1218, 1216, 576, 8060, 8061 Algebra Index Copyright © 2025 Rod Pierce
